name: Kander
stretch: Kander cut at Strättligen, into Lake Thun
summary: Bern led the Kander through a hill into Lake Thun to stop floods in the villages below Thun.

stops.title: The Kander before 1714
text: Before 1714 the Kander did not flow into Lake Thun. The red dashed line shows its old course: north through the valley of today's Glütschbach, then across the Thun Allmend (common pasture). It joined the Aare below Thun, opposite the mouth of the Zulg.

The red area shows the wide gravel bed on the Allmend. The river carried much gravel and had little slope here. It often flooded Thierachern, Uetendorf, Uttigen and other villages, and its gravel pushed water back up the Aare to Thun.
The lower part of the line is approximate. Switch on the historical map of 1890 to see the old river bed. The old bed is still marked there as 'Kandergrund'.

stops.title: A tunnel through the hill
text: Bern decided to lead the Kander into Lake Thun. The map maker Samuel Bodmer made the plan.

From 1711 to 1713 about 300 day workers and 100 forced labourers dug a tunnel of about 250 m through the Strättlig hill. In August 1714 the hill above the tunnel fell in. The river then quickly cut a deep gorge backwards into the land.
The blue line shows the new short course through the gorge into the lake. The red dashed line shows the long old course to the Aare, which became dry.

lines.name: Kander since 1714: through the Strättlig hill into Lake Thun
Old course of the Kander before 1714: Glütsch valley and across the Thun Allmend to the Aare (lower part approximate)

stops.title: Now Thun is flooded
text: All the Kander water now came into Lake Thun. The lake rose, and the town of Thun had big floods.

From 1720 to 1726 Thun made the Aare canal (the 'new Aare') wider and opened it. It also rebuilt bridges and the town water works. Work on the locks in Thun and on the Aare down to Bern went on for about 150 years.
The blue line shows where the Kander water now enters the lake. The red dashed line shows the old course, which no longer brought water to the Aare below Thun.

stops.title: Gravel from the delta
text: The Kander built a delta (new land made of river gravel) into Lake Thun. The blue line shows the river across this delta.

Since 1913 the company Kanderkies AG takes gravel from the delta, so the delta has kept about the same size. In 1930 a church meeting centre was built on the delta, today the Gwatt-Zentrum. In 1974 a nature area, the Unterer Kandergrien, was made at the lake.

text: Blue: the Kander today, through the gorge of 1714 into Lake Thun. Red: the old course before 1714.
The old valley to the north is now farmland, roads and houses. Only the small Glütschbach flows there.

Area traced by hand on the 1890 map. New line from OpenStreetMap. Length 1 km is from the HLS table.
why: The Kander comes down from the Bernese Oberland with much gravel. Before 1714 it ran across the flat land west of Thun and joined the Aare below the town. There its gravel raised the bed and blocked the Aare. Fields and villages such as Thierachern, Uetendorf and Uttigen were flooded again and again, and the land along the Aare became marsh.
The government of Bern decided to lead the river into Lake Thun, where the gravel could settle in deep water. The work of 1711 to 1714 was paid and led by Bern, after a plan by Samuel Bodmer.

The work solved one problem and made new ones. The tunnel fell in, and the river cut a deep gorge. Lake Thun now got much more water, and Thun suffered floods. Bern had to widen the Aare outflow in Thun and work on it for a long time. The Kander diversion is one of the first big river works in Europe made on purpose to change a river's course.

name: Linth
stretch: Lake Walen to Lake Zurich (with the Escher canal from Mollis)
summary: The Linth was led into Lake Walen and a new canal was dug to Lake Zurich, to end floods, marshes and malaria in the Linth plain.

stops.title: A plain of marsh and fever
text: Before 1807 the Linth flowed from Mollis to Ziegelbrücke. There it met the Maag, the outflow of Lake Walen. Then it wound through the Linth plain to Lake Zurich. The red dashed line shows this old course.

From the 1750s gravel from the Linth blocked the Maag. Lake Walen rose, and Weesen and Walenstadt were flooded again and again. The plain became a marsh (red area near Tuggen). Malaria (a fever spread by mosquitoes) hit the villages.

The long red line comes from a plan of 1811 and is approximate. The short red lines near Tuggen are old river arms that were still on the map in 1890. Switch on the historical map of 1854 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: The Escher canal
text: Andreas Lanz from Bern had the idea in 1783: lead the Linth into Lake Walen. The lake would catch the gravel.
The work began in 1807. Johann Gottfried Tulla from Baden helped with the plan. Hans Conrad Escher led the work with Conrad Schindler.
In 1811 the Escher canal opened (blue line). It is about 5 km long and leads the Linth from Mollis straight into Lake Walen. The red dashed line shows the old bed to Ziegelbrücke.

stops.title: The Linth canal
text: In 1816 the Linth canal opened (blue line). It leads the water from Lake Walen straight through the plain to Lake Zurich, at Grynau.

The red dashed line shows the winding old river. The new canal is much shorter and steeper, so the water flows away faster. The level of Lake Walen went down, and the towns on the lake were safe from the yearly floods.

text: The marsh in the plain was drained step by step (red area: the old marsh near Tuggen). The upper plain became farmland during the Second World War. The lower plain followed until 1965.
From 1862 to 2003 a federal Linth commission looked after the canals. Since 2004 the cantons Glarus, Schwyz, St. Gallen and Zurich do this together.

HLS table gives 15 km; HLS Linth article 17 km and 1807–1823.
why: In the 18th century the Linth brought more and more gravel from the Glarus valleys. Forests were cut, and floods became worse. At Ziegelbrücke the gravel blocked the Maag, the outflow of Lake Walen. Lake Walen rose by several metres, and Weesen and Walenstadt stood in water for weeks. The whole plain to Lake Zurich became a marsh with malaria. People lost fields and many became poor.

Andreas Lanz proposed in 1783 to lead the Linth into Lake Walen. In 1804 the Tagsatzung (the meeting of the cantons) decided to do the work. It was paid mostly by shares that people all over Switzerland bought. Hans Conrad Escher of Zurich led the work from 1807 without pay. After his death in 1823 his family got the name 'Escher von der Linth'.

The Linth correction was the first big work of the whole Swiss nation. Later, people saw that straight canals also take away space for nature. Since 2008 the Linth works have been renewed, with more room for the river in some places.

name: Gürbe
summary: The canton of Bern put the meandering Gürbe into a straight canal and drained the marshy Gürbe valley.

stops.title: A wet valley floor
text: The Gürbe comes from the Gantrisch area and flows north to the Aare near Belp. In the valley it had little slope and made many bends. The red dashed line shows the winding old bed between Kaufdorf and Belp.

In the 18th century people cut forests in the mountains for pastures. After that the river flooded more often. The wet valley floor was used for grazing. The villages and roads stayed on the dry slopes.
Switch on the historical map of 1870 to see the old river bed.

lines.name: Winding old bed of the Gürbe between Kaufdorf and Belp, traced on the 1870 map (one loop near 46.85 N slightly cut)

stops.title: The Gürbe canal
text: In 1854 the canton took over the river work. From 1855 a straight canal (a river bed dug by people) was built, with side ditches to drain the valley. The main stretch from Wattenwil to the Aare was done by 1865.
The blue line shows the straight canal. The red dashed line shows the old bends. In the mountains people planted forests and built check dams to hold back the gravel.

lines.name: Gürbe canal (straight bed since 1855–1865)
Winding old bed of the Gürbe between Kaufdorf and Belp, traced on the 1870 map (one loop near 46.85 N slightly cut)

stops.title: Fields and an airfield
text: The lower valley was drained for farming in 1917–1923, the middle valley in 1942–1951. The Gürbetal railway opened in 1901–1902.
In 1929 the airfield Belpmoos was built on the former marsh near the mouth. The blue line shows the canal that made this land dry.

lines.name: Gürbe canal (straight bed since 1855–1865)

stops.title: The Gürbe today
text: Blue: the Gürbe today. Red: the old winding bed. Many villages in the lower valley now belong to the Bern area. Floods still happen sometimes, for example in 1990.
After big floods, the mouth of the Gürbe was rebuilt in 2006, and the floodplain forest was made more natural again.

lines.name: Gürbe canal (straight bed since 1855–1865)
Winding old bed of the Gürbe between Kaufdorf and Belp, traced on the 1870 map (one loop near 46.85 N slightly cut)

notes: Old bed traced on the 1870 Dufour map (no earlier tile of this series covers the valley). Upper valley (Wattenwil–Kaufdorf) not drawn: the old course is not clear on the map. New line from OpenStreetMap ('Gürbe'). HLS Gürbe article dates the canal works 1855–1911; HLS table gives 1855–65 for Wattenwil–Aare. Federal subsidy sentence is general (HLS Flusskorrektionen).
why: The Gürbe is a short but wild stream. In heavy rain it brings much gravel from the steep Gantrisch slopes. In the flat valley below Wattenwil it slowed down, made bends and flooded the valley floor. The land was wet and good only for pasture.

In 1854 the canton of Bern took over the river works from the villages. Bern paid for a straight canal and for check dams and new forests in the mountains. Later work used federal money after the laws on water works (1877) and forests (1876).
The canal made the valley dry, so farms, a railway and later an airfield could be built. Today the canton gives the river more room again at some places, for flood safety and nature.

name: Nozon / Orbe
stretch: Orny and Orbe to Lake Neuchâtel
summary: Vaud put the Orbe and the Nozon between dams to drain the marshy Orbe plain and fight marsh fever.

stops.title: The Orbe marsh
text: For centuries the Orbe plain between Orbe and Yverdon was a marsh (red area). The river, here called the Thièle, wound slowly through it to Lake Neuchâtel (red dashed line). Floods were common, and many people had marsh fever (malaria).
In 1854 the Grand Council of Vaud decided to put the Orbe between dams. Switch on the historical map of 1850 to see the old river bed.

areas.name: Orbe marsh (Grand Marais) before the correction (approximate outline, 1850 map)

stops.title: Canals and lower lakes
text: From 1856 new straight canals were dug through the plain, for the Orbe and for the Nozon from Orny. The blue line shows the straight canal. The red dashed line shows the old bends near Ependes.
The first Jura water correction (1868–1891) lowered Lake Neuchâtel. This helped the water to flow away from the plain. The marsh fever went back, and new farmland came.

stops.title: A prison farm on new land
text: In 1899 the prison of Bochuz was built on the new land, with its own farm.
There were fewer floods and less bank erosion (land washed away at the banks). The blue line shows the canal next to the new farmland.

stops.title: The plain today
text: Blue: the canals today. Red: the old river and the old marsh. In 1962–1973 the second Jura water correction lowered Lake Neuchâtel again.
Drainage made the peat soil (soil made of old plant matter) shrink and sink. Some farmland was lost. Some valuable wetlands still exist.

The 1850 map already shows a straight Orbe channel in the upper plain (an earlier work), so the old line there follows that channel. Coloured Siegfried sheets for this area start about 1895, so stop 2 now uses 1895. No source found with details of the Nozon works. New lines from OpenStreetMap ('La Thièle', "L'Orbe").
why: The Orbe plain is very flat and lies only a little above Lake Neuchâtel. The river had almost no slope, so water stayed on the land. The plain was a marsh with peat, and marsh fever (malaria) was common in the villages around it.

In 1854 the Grand Council of Vaud decided to correct the Orbe. From 1856 the canton dug canals and built dams. The work was linked to the first Jura water correction, which lowered the lake from 1868 to 1891; without the lower lake, the canals could not drain the plain well.
The plain became farmland. But drained peat shrinks, so the soil sank and some fields became wet again. Today some wetlands are protected.

name: Alpine Rhine (Landquart–Rüthi)
summary: St. Gallen, with federal money, put the wide, braided Rhine between straight dams from Bad Ragaz to Au (1862-1883), to stop floods and to win dry farmland.

stops.title: The natural Alpine Rhine
text: Before about 1860 no dams held the Rhine in the valley from Reichenau to Lake Constance. The river ran in a wide gravel bed, in places more than 500 m wide. It split into many channels around gravel banks and islands, and it moved its channel after each big flood.

Below Au the river made long bends: around Diepoldsau and Hohenems, past Lustenau and Brugg, then west to Gaissau and Rheineck. It reached Lake Constance at Altenrhein, about 8 km west of today's mouth.

The red line and the red area are traced on the oldest swisstopo maps, the Dufour sheets of 1850 to 1854. The red line is the main channel; the red area is the whole gravel bed. The red area is the whole gravel bed.

stops.title: Dams at Buchs and Sevelen
text: St. Gallen passed a law for a full Rhine correction in 1853. In 1862 the federal parliament agreed to pay one third of the cost. From 1862 the engineers Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann and later Jost Wey built the works from Bad Ragaz to Au.

They built two straight dams. The water now ran in one channel between them. At Buchs and Sevelen you see the new dams (blue) and the old, wide bed (red) next to each other. Switch on the historical map of 1876 to see both on the map of that time.

stops.title: A straight river
text: By 1883 the dams reached from Bad Ragaz to Au. The old side arms dried out. Farmers made fields and meadows on the old gravel bed.

But the dams closed the river off, so the side streams could not flow into the Rhine any more. So the Werdenberg inland canal (a river bed dug by people) was built in 1882-1886. It collects the small streams and leads them along the valley. In 1885-1887 the first large land improvement in Switzerland drained the land at Haag near Sennwald.

stops.title: The bend at Oberriet
text: Further down, at Oberriet and Kriessern, the old river swung in wide curves inside its gravel bed. The new dams cut through these curves in an even line.
The red lines show the old bends; the blue line is the new, straight channel. Switch on the historical map of 1900 to see the old gravel banks next to the new channel.

stops.title: The Rhine valley today
text: Today the valley floor is farmland, villages, roads and industry. The natural river and most wetlands are gone. In 1890 there were 6039 ha of moorland, in 1999 only 106 ha.

The dams did not end all danger. In 1927 the Rhine broke its dam above the railway bridge at Schaan and flooded the Liechtenstein lowland. Between 1953 and 1972 so much gravel was taken from the river that its bed sank by 4 to 5 m.

notes: Old course and gravel bed traced on the Dufour sheets (first edition 1850-1854; map edition 1862 used because it covers both banks). Dufour sheets are less exact than later maps; the red line can be off by 50-100 m. HLS table: 1860-90 Landquart-Rüthi; HLS Rhein article: Ragaz-Au 1862-1883. Haag position approximate. The wide area also includes some gravel banks drawn beside the bed.
why: The Rhine brings much gravel from the mountains of Graubünden. In the flat valley the water slowed down and dropped the gravel. So the river bed and the ground water rose, and the fields beside the river became wet. The river had big floods, for example in 1566 and 1762, and many floods between 1817 and 1890.

For centuries each village protected itself with a 'Wuhr' (a short dam of stone and wood that pushes the water away from the bank). But a Wuhr on one bank pushed the water to the other bank. So the villages of St. Gallen, Liechtenstein and Vorarlberg quarrelled about their Wuhre for hundreds of years. In 1847 St. Gallen and Liechtenstein agreed on fixed bank lines and a river width of 120 m.

After many flood years from 1846 to 1856, St. Gallen passed a Rhine law in 1853. From 1862 the Swiss federal state paid one third of the cost. The engineers Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann and Jost Wey built continuous dams from Bad Ragaz to Au (1862-1883). Inland canals and drainage followed.

The work gave dry farmland and safer villages. But it also destroyed almost all floodplains and moors. Later, gravel mining lowered the bed too much. The dam break near Schaan in 1927 showed that the dams were not safe everywhere.

name: Rhône (Rotten)
summary: After the floods of 1860 the Rhône was put between dams from Brig to Lake Geneva; two more corrections followed because the bed kept rising.

stops.title: Marshes in the Rhône plain
text: The Rhône often changed its bed. Between Martigny and Riddes it spread over a wide bed of gravel, with side arms, islands and marshes (red area). The red dashed line shows the main channel in 1862.

Since the 16th century villages built simple dams of brushwood, earth and gravel. They helped little. Big floods came in 1469, 1640, 1740, 1778 and 1860. Switch on the historical map of 1862 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: Many arms at the delta
text: Near Lake Geneva the Rhône split into several arms (red dashed lines) and built a wide delta (new land made of river gravel). The red area shows the old delta with its islands and wet woods.
Floods changed the arms from year to year. The land between Chessel, Noville and Le Bouveret was wet and hard to use. Switch on the historical map of 1850 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: The first correction
text: After the floods of 1860, the Rhône from Brig to Lake Geneva was corrected from 1863. Two dams were built 70 to 120 m apart. Short cross walls (groynes) pointed into the river and made a narrow main channel.

The blue line shows the river between its dams. The red dashed line and the red area show the old wide bed. For the first time the canton of Valais got federal money for a building project. Over time about 7000 ha of farmland were won for vines, fruit and vegetables.

stops.title: The second correction
text: The river could not carry all the gravel from its side streams to the lake. The bed rose again. Floods came in 1897 and 1935.

In the second correction (about 1930–1960) workers removed gravel from the bed and made the dams stronger and higher. Between Sierre and Martigny they joined the ends of the groynes to a firm bank (1928–1961). The blue line shows this fixed channel.

stops.title: The third correction begins
text: Floods in 1987, 1993 and 2000 showed that the dams were not safe enough. Some old dams broke.

The third Rhône correction started in 2009 in Visp, to protect the town and its large chemical industry. The blue line shows the Rhône at Visp. The river gets more space, and its bed is made lower or wider.

stops.title: The Rhône today
text: Blue: the Rhône today, in one straight channel to Lake Geneva. Red: the old arms and the wide old delta.
Today the Rhône plain is full of towns, roads, industry and farms. The third correction goes on step by step until about 2040.

notes: Dates differ: HLS table 1863–84, HLS Rhone article 1863–1894, canton 1863–1894; second correction HLS 1930–1960, canton 1936–1961. 'Until about 2040' is from a news summary of the canton plan (2020–2039 second stage), not checked on the canton page. The 1870 map already shows the first dams near Fully (work started 1863). Lines: old main channel Martigny–Riddes traced on the 1862 Dufour map (the 1870 sheet already shows first dams near Fully); delta arms placed by hand on the 1850 Dufour map; areas drawn by hand (approximate). New lines from OpenStreetMap ('Le Rhône', 'Rotten'). Farmers' protests against land loss for the third correction: general knowledge, not checked in a source.
why: The Rhône carries much gravel from the glaciers and side valleys. In the flat main valley of Valais it spread out, changed its bed and made marshes. The plain was a danger for health (marsh fever) and for traffic, and little of it could be farmed. Villages protected themselves with small dams, often at the cost of the next village.

The great flood of 1860 started the first correction. Valais asked the young federal state for money, and in 1863 the Confederation agreed to pay part of the work. It was one of the first federal subsidies for a building project. The federal laws of 1874–1877 later made the Confederation a regular partner for river works.

Because the bed kept rising with gravel, a second correction followed (about 1930–1960). After the floods of 1987, 1993 and 2000, Valais and Vaud began the third correction in 2009. It gives the river more width and lowers its bed. It also brings back some natural river banks, but it needs farmland, which led to protests by farmers.

name: Aare in the Hasli valley
summary: The Aare below Meiringen was put into a straight canal and Lake Brienz was lowered to dry the marshy valley floor.

stops.title: Floods in the Hasli valley
text: The Aare between Meiringen and Lake Brienz often flooded the valley floor. Much of the land was marsh and hard to farm.

Near the lake the river made a big loop to the south side of the valley (red dashed line). One reason for the floods was the large need for wood of the iron mines in the valley: cut forests let more water and gravel run down. Switch on the historical map of 1864 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: A straight Aare
text: From 1866 the Aare was put into a straight bed between dams (blue line). The loop near the lake (red dashed line) was cut off.
The valley floor became dry enough for meadows and fields.

stops.title: The Hasli valley today
text: Blue: the straight Aare today, past farmland and the airfield of Meiringen. Red: the old loop near the lake.
The canton plans more room for the river for flood safety and nature.

notes: HLS table: 1866–75; HLS Oberhasli article: 1866–1880. The 1854 law is from a secondary source (Hasli chronicle via plattformj.ch), not HLS. Last sentence on canton plans is general; not checked in detail. The 1864 map already shows a straight Aare from Brienzwiler to Meiringen; only the loop near the lake is drawn as old course. The claim that Lake Brienz was lowered was removed from the text: not confirmed in a high-trust source. New line from OpenStreetMap ('Aare').
why: The Hasli valley floor between Meiringen and Lake Brienz is flat, and the Aare brings gravel from the high Alps. The river wound across the valley, flooded it often and kept it wet. Farmers could use little of the land.

The canton of Bern decided to correct the river and dry the valley. The work of 1866 to 1875 gave the Aare a straight bed between dams. After the federal laws of 1876–1877 the Confederation helped to pay for river and forest works in the mountains.
The straight canal made the land dry, so meadows, fields and later an airfield could be made. Today the canton plans to give the river more space again, for flood safety and nature.

The doctor Johann Rudolf Schneider from Nidau pushed for a big solution for decades. The engineer Richard La Nicca made the plan. In 1867 the federal parliament agreed to pay part of the costs, and the cantons Bern, Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Solothurn paid the rest. The Nidau–Büren canal was one of the main works of 1868–1891.

The canal lowered the lakes by about 2.5 m. But the drained peat soil sank, and floods came back. So the canal was widened in the second correction of 1962–1973, and the weir at Port now regulates the lakes.

why: The Seeland between the three Jura lakes is very flat. The Aare from Aarberg brought much gravel and flowed slowly to Meienried. There it blocked the Zihl, the outflow of Lake Biel. At high water the lakes rose and flooded the Grosses Moos and the land down to Solothurn. People suffered from floods, wet fields, poor harvests and marsh fever.

Johann Rudolf Schneider, a doctor from Nidau, fought for a solution from the 1830s. Richard La Nicca's plan (1842) led the Aare into Lake Biel through the Hagneck canal, so the lake could catch the gravel and the floods, and lowered all three lakes. The federal decree of 1867 paid a large part, the cantons Bern, Fribourg, Vaud, Neuchâtel and Solothurn the rest. The work ran from 1868 to 1891.

The lakes went down by about 2.5 m, and new land came out of the water, including the land bridge to St. Peter's Island. But the drained peat shrank, so the land sank and floods came back. The second correction (1962–1973) widened the canals. Today the soil loss in the Grosses Moos and the loss of wetlands are the main problems.

Bern ordered the villages to build dams ('Schwellen'). But one village's dam often pushed the water to the other bank. After bad floods Bern made rules for the whole river in 1766–1768. After 1800 forests were cut, and floods became worse. Switch on the historical map of 1870 to see the old river bed.

why: The Emme drains the steep hills of the Emmental. After storms it rises very fast and brings much gravel. For centuries it changed its bed and covered fields with gravel. Poor people lived on the risky flat land along the river.
For a long time each village built its own dams, and often pushed the water to the neighbours. Bern made common rules in 1766–1768. After 1800 many forests were cut, and the floods got worse.

The federal laws on forests (1876) and water works (1877) brought federal money from 1884. Forests were planted and the river was put between dams. The narrow bed made the river cut deeper, so today the banks need constant repair, and the cantons give the Emme more room in some places.

why: The Thur often left its bed, mostly in its middle course. Big floods came in 1664, 1755, 1789, 1852, 1876, 1881 and 1883. The water covered fields and villages in the flat valley between Thurgau and Zurich.

From 1874 to 1893, the communes along the river in Thurgau and Zurich worked together on one project, the Thur correction. Workers cut through the bends and built dams, so the river ran in a straight channel. The floods of 1876 and 1881 came while this work was going on. Both cantons gave money. The Thurgau state archive keeps files on federal subsidies for the Thur correction from 1885 and 1893. A federal subsidy is money from the Swiss state; the 1877 federal law on water works made such payments possible. Near the mouth, Zurich says a 5 km canal from Kleinandelfingen to the Rhine was built in about 1860.
The straight river did not stop all floods. Dams broke again in 1910, 1965, 1977 and 1978. The canton of Zurich also says that the protection works upstream sent more water down to the lower Thur.

In 1979 the three cantons on the river made a common plan. From 1983 to 2005, Zurich rebuilt the Thur from the Thurgau border to Andelfingen in a more natural way, in five stages. From 2008 to 2017, the project at the Thur mouth gave the river space again. Now it can make bends and flood its floodplain (the low land next to a river that water covers in a flood). The Thurauen are the largest floodplain area of the Swiss Mittelland, with almost 400 ha.

why: The Glatt flows out of Lake Greifensee and has very little slope in its upper course. So the water moved slowly, and the land along it was wet and marshy. Mills on the river were often in danger from high water. The city of Zurich controlled the river from the 15th century, and a first attempt to correct it came in 1593.

In 1807 the canton rejected a plan with dams on the sides (the 'Vogel project'). In 1812 the cantonal water police commission (an office that watched over rivers and water works) made an expert report, with help from Hans Conrad Escher. Workers dug a tunnel near Rheinsfelden and made the river straighter and deeper between Glattbrugg and Oberglatt. But in 1825 the money ran out and the work stopped. The project was closed in 1840.

The second correction came from 1878 to 1895. The third correction started in 1936. It prepared the ground for the planned airport at Kloten, for new houses and for melioration (work that makes wet land dry and good for farming). It also gave work to people without jobs. A last correction from Niederglatt to the Rhine in 1975 ended the old water power plants on the lower river.

Today the federal and cantonal authorities say that the corrections forced the Glatt into a narrow, deep and straight bed with hard banks. The river had flowed in bends through a wide area of moor and floodplain. That landscape was lost, and the river has large ecological problems. Since 2011, federal law tells the cantons to bring such rivers back to a more natural state. Projects at the airport and at other places now give the Glatt more space.

In 1876 a very large flood caused huge damage along the Töss. Another flood came in 1877. The Zurich government then acted in two ways. The sills are dangerous for people and stop fish from moving up the river. The straight bed is a poor home for plants and animals. In 2018 the canton and the communes made a plan to give the Töss a more natural form over the next decades.

In 1868 a very bad flood killed 41 people. The railway across the plain opened in 1874. Both gave new force to plans for a correction.

why: The Ticino and the streams that join it often flooded. The river also changed its bed again and again. In the Magadino plain this made marshes. For centuries the plain was almost empty, because people could not farm it and it was not healthy to live there. Malaria (a fever that mosquitoes carry) was known there from the 15th century and stayed a problem until the end of the 19th century.

Plans to correct the river go back to the early 19th century. Two events started the real work. In 1868 a very bad flood killed 41 people and caused more than 6 million francs of damage. In 1874 the railway from Locarno to Bellinzona opened across the plain.

The cantonal government made two projects. Parliament accepted them by a small majority, but the people voted no. The north of the canton (Sopraceneri) was for them, the south (Sottoceneri) was against. The government still set up a consortium in 1886. A consortium is a group of land owners and public bodies who share the work and the cost. The correction was approved in 1885 and started in 1888. It went on, with breaks, into the 20th century and cost more than 11 million francs.

The river now ran between dams. This made it possible to drain the plain in four big steps from 1918 to 1961. The Magadino plain became the largest farming area of the canton. Later, houses, roads, shops and the airfield also took much of the new land. In 1974 the canton protected the Bolle di Magadino at the river mouth as a nature reserve.

summary: Switzerland and Austria cut two big bends of the Rhine, at Fussach (1900) and Diepoldsau (1923), and moved its mouth into Lake Constance, to make the river shorter, faster and safer.

stops.title: The old mouth at Altenrhein
text: Until 1900 the Rhine flowed from Au north to Brugg, then west past St. Margrethen and Gaissau, and through Rheineck into Lake Constance at Altenrhein. On this long way the water lost speed, and the gravel filled the bed.

Plans for a shorter course existed since 1792. In 1838 Friedrich Wilhelm Hartmann proposed a cut from Lustenau straight to Fussach. The red line is the old course just before the work. Switch on the historical map of 1895 to see it.

lines.name: Old Rhine to Altenrhein (river course until 1900, traced on the 1895 map)

stops.title: The Fussach cut
text: The state treaty of 1892 between Switzerland and Austria-Hungary created the International Rhine Regulation (IRR). In 1895-1900 the IRR dug a new, straight bed of about 5 km in Austria, from Brugg near Lustenau to the lake at Fussach. It made the river about 7 km shorter.
The old Rhine to Altenrhein became a quiet side water. Today it takes the water of the Rhine valley inland canal (built 1895-1906).

stops.title: The loop at Diepoldsau
text: Upstream, the Rhine still made a big loop to the east around Diepoldsau, close to Hohenems. Here the river flowed slowly, gravel settled, and the bed rose.
The 1892 treaty also planned a second cut here. The red line follows the loop as it was before the work began. Switch on the historical map of 1905 to see its gravel banks.

stops.title: The Diepoldsau cut
text: In 1910-1923 the IRR dug a straight new bed west of Diepoldsau, from Kriessern to Widnau. The First World War delayed the work. On 18 April 1923 the water first flowed through the cut. It made the river about 3 km shorter.

The old loop became the 'Alter Rhein', a quiet water. Since then Diepoldsau lies between the new Rhine and the old loop, which is still the border with Austria. A new treaty in 1924 settled the further works.

stops.title: Today and the Rhesi project
text: The mouth was pushed into the lake with new dams (1924-1934 and since 1972), so that the gravel goes to deep water. A treaty of 1954 made the middle channel narrower, so that the water flows faster and carries the gravel away.

The dams are still too weak for the biggest floods. In the project Rhesi, Switzerland and Austria will widen the river bed on 26 km, from the Ill mouth to the lake, for more safety and more nature. The new state treaty came into force on 1 July 2025. The project was submitted for approval in May 2026. It will cost about CHF 2 billion.

why: Below Au the Rhine made long bends before it reached Lake Constance at Altenrhein. On this long, flat way the water lost speed and dropped its gravel. The bed rose, the dams had to be built higher and higher, and the land behind them became wet. Big floods hit the St. Gallen Rhine valley in 1868, and the Vorarlberg side in 1888 and 1890.

The river is the border between Switzerland and Austria. A cut through a bend helps both sides, but each state had to give land and money. Talks started in 1824, after the floods of 1817 and 1821, and plans for cuts existed since 1792. But for almost 70 years the two states did not agree.

After the floods of 1888 and 1890 they signed a state treaty in 1892. It created the International Rhine Regulation (IRR), which both states pay for. The IRR built the Fussach cut (1895-1900) and the Diepoldsau cut (1910-1923). Together with the earlier works the river became about 10 km shorter, and the mouth moved about 8 km to the east. Treaties of 1924 and 1954 added the dams into the lake and a narrower middle channel.
The cuts made the valley much safer, but the river lost its natural banks. Today the IRR and the two states plan the project Rhesi to give the river more room again.

name: Muota
summary: After the flood of 1910 the Muota was corrected in two stretches, in the Muota valley and on the plain from Ibach to Brunnen.

stops.title: The Muota before the flood of 1910
text: Since the 15th century, groups of land owners slowly pushed the Muota into a fixed bed. This let the harbour village of Brunnen grow. Before, houses stood only on the higher ground.
In June 1910 a great flood destroyed bridges, houses and stables in the Muota valley.

stops.title: The correction
text: In 1910 the canton of Schwyz accepted money from the federal state. In the years after 1910 it built up the Muota from above Muotathal to the lake (blue line). The federal state, the canton and the district of Schwyz paid subsidies. The land owners paid the rest.
Between Ibach and Brunnen the course changed little, because the bed was already fixed.

Muota in the Muota valley today (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: The Muota today

lines.name: Muota today, in its secured bed (OpenStreetMap)

notes: The dates 1911–1926 are not confirmed. A Federal Court ruling of 1931 says the works were done "in the years after 1910"; the cost list was fixed in November 1922, so the stop uses 1922. Round 2: no old line is drawn, because the maps of 1854, 1900 and 1935 show nearly the same course between Ibach and Brunnen and in the valley; only the new course (OpenStreetMap) is shown.
why: The Muota flows from the Muotatal through the Schwyz valley basin and into Lake Lucerne at Brunnen. It damaged its valley many times. Its flood plain kept the village of Brunnen on the hill sides for a long time. From the 15th century, groups of land owners built and kept river banks, and the river was slowly forced into a fixed bed.
The last big flood came in June 1910. In the commune of Muotathal it destroyed 7 bridges, 11 houses and 4 stables, and many people became very poor.

In 1910 the canton of Schwyz accepted a federal subsidy for the work. With this, the canton took on the duty to build the works and to keep them in good condition. In the years after 1910 the canton built up the Muota from above Muotatal down to the lake. The federal state, the canton and the district of Schwyz paid subsidies. The land owners who had a benefit paid the rest. In 1922 the district also asked the Korporation Uri to pay, because it owned alps in the Muota area in the canton of Uri. Uri said no. In 1931 the Federal Council and the Federal Court agreed with Uri.

A Wuhrkorporation (a group of land owners who must keep the river dams in good condition) was founded and kept the dams. Today the district of Schwyz plans to give the Muota a more natural bed near the old Brunnen power plant.

why: In the Intyamon valley the Saane flows over a flat valley floor. It brought much gravel and spread over a wide bed with many arms. Floods took land from the farmers, and much of the valley floor was only gravel and bushes.

From the end of the 19th century the villages and the canton of Fribourg narrowed the river between dams to win farmland. Federal money for river works was possible after the law of 1877. The work went on in many steps until 1987.
The narrow river is safer for the fields. But the wide gravel banks, a rich natural habitat, were mostly lost.

name: Areuse
summary: The Areuse in the Val-de-Travers was corrected to protect the valley floor from floods.

stops.title: The Areuse in the Val-de-Travers
text: The Areuse is the main river of the canton of Neuchâtel. In the Val-de-Travers it flows through a flat valley floor. A first large correction was made in 1867–1869.
Below Travers the river still made wide bends in 1940, for example near Le Loclat (red dashed line). Switch on the historical map of 1940 to see the old river bed.

stops.title: The second correction
text: From 1949 to 1955 the river was corrected between Travers and Couvet. The bends were cut off, and the river got a straighter bed (blue line). More works followed until 1984.

Old bends of the Areuse between Travers and Bois de Croix, before 1949–1955 (traced on the 1940 map)

stops.title: The Areuse today

Below Noiraigue the Areuse flows through its wild gorge. The water of its area gives drinking water to about 70% of the people of the canton.

why: The Val-de-Travers has a flat, wet valley floor. The Areuse flooded it often, and parts of it were marsh. The river was corrected a first time in 1867–1869.
After the Second World War the canton of Neuchâtel corrected the river again (1949–1955), to protect the villages and to win dry farmland. Work went on until 1984.
The straighter river is safer for the valley. Today the canton also restores parts of the Areuse to make them more natural.

name: Reuss in Uri
summary: Uri put the Reuss into a straight canal to the lake, which won farmland; in 1985 a natural delta was made again.

stops.title: The Reuss canal
text: The Reuss often flooded the flat valley floor between Altdorf and Lake Uri. A special court for water works is known from 1493.

From 1850 to 1863 the Reuss was put into a straight canal (blue line) from the Attinghausen bridge down to the lake. More land could be farmed. No map we found shows the old river course before 1850, so no red line is drawn. Switch on the historical map of 1899 to see the canal and the marshy delta beside it.

stops.title: The canal reaches the lake

Since 1891 companies take about 100,000 m3 of gravel each year out of the lake. The red line is the lake shore of 1899.

notes: Not in the HLS table. Length "c. 4.5 km" measured on today's map. No map or plan before 1850 of the old Reuss course or delta was found (swisstopo series starts with Dufour sheets that already show the canal; the 1864 tiles are also shifted by several hundred metres here, so they were not used for tracing). The 1925 map shows almost no change at the mouth compared with 1899, so the 1900–1912 extension is not clearly visible. The 1899 shore line was traced on the 1899 map. The new delta of 1985 is shown on today's map.
why: The Reuss is the main river of the canton of Uri. It often flooded the flat valley floor between Altdorf and Lake Uri. Because of this, land owners formed groups to build and keep river banks. A special court for water works on the Reuss and the Schächen is known from 1493. The state of Uri paid part of the costs.

From 1850 to 1863 the Reuss was put into a canal from the Attinghausen bridge down to the plain. From 1900 to 1912 the canal was made longer at the mouth. The straight river gave more land for farming. In the first half of the 20th century the plain on both sides was drained. In 1891 the river became property of the canton.

The Reuss carries about 100,000 m3 of gravel each year. Since 1891 companies have taken this gravel out of the lake. The dredging ate away the shore. Land of the Korporation Uri at the delta became smaller and smaller.

In 1985 the canton of Uri made a law on the Reuss delta. The canal was made shorter and two side arms were opened. Now the Reuss flows into the lake in three branches and can build a natural delta again. Gravel extraction had to stop the loss of land, and new islands were made in the lake. In August 1987 a big flood broke the dams and covered large parts of the Uri valley floor. From 1995 to 1999 the canton built new flood protection between Flüelen and Attinghausen.

name: Reuss plain (Aargau)
summary: The Reusstal renovation corrected the river, drained the valley floor for farming and created the Flachsee nature reserve.

stops.title: A wandering river
text: Above and below Bremgarten the Reuss made many bends. It flooded the valley and changed its bed. Bank works by the villagers from the 16th century helped little. At Rottenschwil an old loop of the river (red line) was already cut off.
Plans to straighten the river in 1648 (Hans Conrad Gyger) and 1809 (Johann Gottfried Tulla) were never built. Works of about 1840 brought no lasting help.

In 1965 the people of Aargau accepted the "Free Reuss" law with a large majority. In 1969 they narrowly accepted the Reuss valley law, which joined flood protection and nature protection.

In 1975 the new Bremgarten-Zufikon power plant raised the water. The Flachsee formed (blue area). It is now a reserve for water birds of national importance.

notes: Not in the HLS table. Length of the corrected stretch not found. Round 2: the river course in this stretch changed little between 1870 and today, so no older main channel is drawn; the red line is the cut-off loop "Stille Reuss" traced on the 1960 map (also visible in 1870). The Flachsee outline is read from the 1960/today maps and is approximate. The 1965 vote count differs between Stiftung Reusstal papers, so no number is given.
why: In the Aargau Reuss valley the river made many bends. The flat valley floor suffered from floods and from changes of the river bed. People built bank protection from the 16th century, but it helped little. Plans to make the Reuss straight, for example by Hans Conrad Gyger in 1648 and by Johann Gottfried Tulla in 1809, were never built. Corrections from about 1840 did not last. In the 19th century, flood dams were built from Mühlau to Rottenschwil.

In 1953 a dam broke at Merenschwand and the flood caused heavy damage. This started a new plan. The first plans were only technical: dry the land for farming. Nature protection groups were against them, because the valley was an important wetland. In 1962 they founded the Stiftung Reusstal (a foundation to protect the Reuss valley).

In 1963 the foundation started a popular initiative, 'Freie Reuss'. In 1965 the people of Aargau accepted it with a large majority. It stopped new power plants on the Reuss below Bremgarten. In 1969 the people accepted the 'Reusstalgesetz' by a small majority. This law joined the river work with nature protection.

From 1971 to 1985 the Reusstalsanierung (the renewal of the Reuss valley) was carried out. It was a project of several cantons that changed the course of the river and drained and improved the land. Agriculture, the electricity industry and nature protection groups all took part. In 1975 the new Bremgarten-Zufikon power plant dammed the river, and the Flachsee was formed. It is now a well-known nature reserve for birds. The power plant also limited the natural movement of the river.

The river builds a large delta (new land made of river gravel) into Lake Maggiore (red area). In 1870 its main arm ran along the Ascona side, and a second arm ran towards Locarno (red lines).

notes: Not in the HLS table. No source gives the year of the straight course across the delta; it is already visible on the 1916 and 1924 maps (and partly on 1893). Round 2: old arms and delta outline traced on the 1870 map; they fit the 1893–1933 maps. The airfield is general knowledge.
why: The Maggia is a wild mountain river. Its water level can rise very fast and very high. Over the centuries it often flooded. Log floating (sending tree trunks down the river) made the floods worse. The worst floods were at Cevio in 1648, with 52 dead, and in 1868, with 41 dead. At its mouth the river carries much gravel and sand into Lake Maggiore. There it builds a large delta that grows all the time, between Locarno and Ascona.

After the floods of 1868 the federal state got new powers. The 1874 constitution gave it the right to supervise water works in the mountains, and the 1877 federal law on water works followed. The federal environment office names the works on the Maggia from 1891 as one of the large corrections of that time.

From 1891 to 1930 a consortium built dams along many parts of the river. A consortium is a group of land owners and public bodies who share the work and the cost. The Maggia was never put into a full canal. A stone bridge between Losone and Solduno, built in 1815 and 1816, was partly destroyed soon after and rebuilt in 1887.

The dams did not stop all floods. In 1951 a flood destroyed the iron bridge at Ponte Brolla, and in 1978 a flood caused much damage. Since 1949, much of the water has gone to hydropower plants. The delta mouth became a nature reserve in 1985.

The Linth correction (1807–1816) lowered Lake Walen by almost 5 m and helped a first time. The red line shows the Seez before its own correction.

why: The Seez comes from the Weisstannental, leaves the valley at Mels and flows about 12 km to Lake Walen at Walenstadt. Floods of the Seez hit Mels in 1750, 1762, 1764 and 1817. At the same time the level of Lake Walen rose more and more. So the floor of the Seez valley turned into marsh.
The Linth correction (from 1807, led by Hans Conrad Escher) lowered Lake Walen by almost 5 m. This was the first help for the Seez valley.

The second step was the Seez correction from 1855 to 1865. A corporation of the land owners and communes, later called the Seezunternehmen, carried out the work to drain the valley. Walenstadt joined it in 1858. The new Seez canal helped industry to start in Walenstadt from 1862. The Seezunternehmen still looks after the river works today.

summary: The Melchaa was led directly into Lake Sarnen, so the lake could catch its gravel.

text: After its gorge, the Grosse Melchaa flowed north-east and joined the Sarneraa below the village of Sarnen (red line). It carried much gravel and wood, and it flooded Sarnen many times.

stops.title: Into the lake
text: Because of these floods, the Melchaa was led into Lake Sarnen in 1880 (blue line). In 1880 the lake shore lay at about the place of today's railway bridge.
This was a small version of the Kander and Linth idea: the lake catches the gravel.

stops.title: Today
text: The gravel now builds a delta in the lake. The river bed rises, by about 1 m in 2005 alone. Lake Sarnen also gets almost one third more water, but its outflow is small. In 2005 the lake reached a record level and flooded large parts of Sarnen.

notes: Not in the HLS table. Year 1880 and reason from an Obwalden government report (2009). Round 2: old course traced on the 1864/1870 map (Dufour-type; the lower part through Sarnen is approximate). The OW report has a site plan of 1880 that was not used.
why: The Grosse Melchaa first flowed north-east after it left its gorge. It joined the Sarneraa below the village of Sarnen. It carried much gravel and wood, and it flooded Sarnen many times and badly.
Because of these repeated floods, the Grosse Melchaa was moved into Lake Sarnen in 1880. In 1880 the shore of the lake was at about the place of the railway bridge today.

The change had side effects. The gravel now builds a delta in the lake. The delta became longer and the slope of the river smaller, so the river can carry less gravel and its bed rises. In 2005 the bed in the lower part rose by about 1 m. Also, the area that drains into Lake Sarnen grew by almost one third. But the Sarneraa, the only outflow of the lake, has a small capacity. Lake Sarnen therefore floods more easily. In 2005 it reached a record level, and the Sarneraa flooded large parts of Sarnen.
